Discover the Nation About Timor-Leste
Southeast Asia's youngest nation is one of its most extraordinary: a place where ancient traditions, pristine nature, and warm hospitality converge at the edge of the Coral Triangle.

A Message from the Minister Welcome to Timor-Leste
It is my great pleasure to welcome you to the official tourism website of Timor-Leste—one of the world’s newest nations and ASEAN’s newest member. Whether you are planning your first visit or returning to discover more, I invite you to use this site as your gateway to the experiences, stories, and people that make our country truly special.
Timor-Leste is blessed with extraordinary natural beauty. At the heart of the Coral Triangle, our waters are among the most biodiverse on Earth, home to vibrant coral reefs, reef fish, sea turtles, whales, and dolphins. From the famed waters of Atauro Island to our pristine beaches, our marine environment offers visitors a rare opportunity to experience nature in an authentic and unspoiled setting.
On land, our mountains, forests, and national parks reveal another side of our diversity. Mount Ramelau, our highest peak, offers inspiring trekking experiences, while Nino Konis Santana National Park—recognised by UNESCO as Timor-Leste’s first Biosphere Reserve—protects important landscapes, seascapes, and wildlife. Across our compact country, visitors can move from rugged mountains to peaceful coastlines and welcoming villages in a single journey.
What I hope you will remember most, however, is the warmth of our people. Timor-Leste’s culture is rich, living, and deeply personal—from sacred houses and tais textiles to traditional music, dance, storytelling, and our renowned organic coffee. Here, hospitality is not a slogan; it is part of who we are.
On behalf of the Government and people of Timor-Leste, I warmly invite you to explore this website, plan your journey, and come experience our country for yourself. We look forward to welcoming you with open hearts to Timor-Leste.
H.E. Francisco Kalbuadi Lay
Vice Prime Minister, Coordinating Minister of Economic Affairs, and Minister of Tourism and Environment of Timor-Leste

History A Story of Resilience
Timor-Leste's history is one of extraordinary endurance. For over 400 years, the island was a Portuguese colony, a period that left deep marks on the culture, language, and architecture, visible today in Dili's colonial churches and the Tetun language, which blends indigenous Austronesian roots with Portuguese.
Following Portugal's withdrawal in 1975, Indonesia invaded and occupied the territory for 24 years, a period marked by widespread suffering and the loss of an estimated 100,000–180,000 lives. The resistance movement, both armed and diplomatic, became one of the defining struggles for self-determination in the late 20th century.
On August 30, 1999, the Timorese people voted overwhelmingly for independence in a UN-supervised referendum. After a period of devastating violence and international intervention, Timor-Leste formally became the world's newest nation on May 20, 2002.
Today, Timor-Leste is building a new chapter. As one of the world's youngest democracies and Southeast Asia's youngest nation, it carries a story of survival and hope that visitors encounter everywhere: in the monuments, the people, and the indomitable spirit that defines the country.
People & Culture Warm Hearts, Living Traditions
With a population of around 1.3 million, Timor-Leste is one of Southeast Asia's most diverse small nations. The country is home to more than 30 indigenous language groups, each with distinct cultural practices, from the mountainous Mambai heartland to the coastal Fataluku communities in the far east.
Catholicism, introduced by the Portuguese, is central to Timorese life; roughly 97% of the population identifies as Catholic, and the country's churches, processions, and feast days are woven into daily rhythms. Yet animist traditions also endure: offerings at sacred lulik houses, harvest ceremonies, and the tara bandu system of customary law that governs natural resources.
Tais weaving is perhaps the most visible cultural art form: intricate hand-woven textiles that carry clan identity, spiritual meaning, and regional pride. Each municipality has distinctive patterns, and a gifted tais is one of the highest forms of respect in Timorese culture.
Music, dance, and oral storytelling remain vital parts of community life. Visitors who attend a village celebration or market day will find a society that is generous, deeply connected to its land, and remarkably welcoming, even in the most remote municipalities.
Geography & Climate Mountains to Coral Reefs
Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of Timor island, the nearby islands of Ataúro and Jaco, and the enclave of Oecusse on the island's northwest coast. Despite its small size (roughly the area of Connecticut), the terrain is astonishingly varied, from sea-level mangroves and white-sand beaches to the 2,963-metre summit of Mount Ramelau.
The central mountain spine runs the length of the country, creating dramatic microclimates: the northern coast is dry and seasonal, while the southern side receives heavy monsoon rains that feed dense tropical forests. The highland plateau around Maubisse and Hatubuilico sits above 1,500 metres, cool enough for sweaters and some of the world's best shade-grown coffee.
Sitting within the Coral Triangle (the global epicentre of marine biodiversity), Timor-Leste's waters harbour extraordinary life. Deep oceanic trenches close to shore bring nutrient-rich upwellings that sustain hundreds of coral species and thousands of fish species, alongside regular whale and dolphin sightings.
The best time to visit is during the dry season (May to November), when roads are more passable and skies clearer, though the early wet season (December–January) brings lush green landscapes and fewer tourists.
Economy A Nation in Transition
Timor-Leste's economy runs on the US dollar, adopted in 2000, with locally minted centavo coins for small change. With a population of around 1.4 million and a GDP near US$1.9 billion, it is one of Asia's smallest and youngest economies and, until recently, the most oil-dependent country in the world.
For two decades, offshore oil and gas underwrote the young state. The Bayu-Undan field in the Timor Sea contributed an estimated US$25 billion in revenue before production ceased in mid-2025. Those proceeds built the Petroleum Fund, a sovereign wealth fund worth roughly US$18 billion that now finances about three-quarters of government spending. The undeveloped Greater Sunrise field, still under negotiation, is the country's next major energy prospect.
Beyond petroleum, daily life turns on agriculture, which employs roughly four in five Timorese. Coffee is the heart of the non-oil export economy: grown under shade in the cool highlands and organic almost by default, Timorese arabica (including the famous Híbrido de Timor, a hybrid discovered here and prized worldwide for its disease resistance) reaches specialty roasters across the US, Australia, Japan and beyond.
The government is betting on diversification across tourism, agriculture and regional integration. In October 2025 Timor-Leste became the 11th member of ASEAN, following its 2024 entry into the World Trade Organization, opening new doors for trade and investment. For visitors, this is a young economy finding its feet: outside the capital, cash (US dollars) is still king, but the warmth of the welcome is constant.

Nature & Wildlife A Biodiversity Hotspot
Timor-Leste's location in the Coral Triangle (the most biodiverse marine region on Earth) gives it an outsized ecological significance. The waters around Ataúro Island alone harbour more reef fish species per site than anywhere else ever recorded, a fact confirmed by Conservation International's groundbreaking 2016 marine survey.
On land, the Nino Konis Santana National Park (the country's first) protects tropical dry forests, coastal ecosystems, and important bird habitat, including several Timor-endemic species. The park spans from the dramatic cliffs of Tutuala to the pristine shores of Jaco Island, the sacred uninhabited island at the country's eastern tip.
Marine megafauna is another draw: between October and December, blue whales, sperm whales, and multiple dolphin species pass through the deep Wetar Strait, making Timor-Leste one of the most accessible whale-watching destinations in Asia.
Conservation is growing: community-led marine protected areas around Ataúro, mangrove restoration projects, and ecotourism initiatives are helping protect these irreplaceable natural assets while creating sustainable livelihoods for local communities.
Portuguese Heritage Four Centuries of Shared History
Portuguese traders first arrived on the island of Timor in the early 16th century, establishing a presence that would endure for over 450 years. Lifau, in what is now the Oecusse enclave, served as the colonial capital from 1702 until it was relocated to Dili in 1769. Portugal's influence shaped the territory through religion, language, architecture, and trade, yet Timorese communities maintained their own traditions, sacred houses, and customary governance throughout. When Portugal withdrew in 1975, Timor-Leste declared independence on 28 November of that year, though Indonesian occupation would delay full sovereignty until 2002.
Across the country, Portuguese-era architecture offers visitors a tangible connection to this layered past. In Dili, the Igreja de Motael, built around 1800 and one of the oldest churches in the country, stands as both a place of worship and a symbol of resistance. The Pousada de Baucau, a restored 1930s Portuguese inn in Baucau's atmospheric old town, offers visitors a chance to stay within colonial-era walls overlooking the sea. The 17th-century fort at Maubara, perched on the coast of Liquiçá, and the fort at Balibo are striking remnants of Portugal's defensive network. Village churches dot the highlands from Maubisse to Ainaro, their whitewashed facades and bell towers a familiar sight against green mountains.
Portugal's most enduring legacy may be the one you hear, taste, and celebrate. Portuguese is one of Timor-Leste's two official languages alongside Tetun, and everyday Tetun is rich with Portuguese loanwords: escola (school), igreja (church), obrigadu (thank you), mesa (table), and janela (window) among hundreds of others. Catholicism, introduced by Dominican and Jesuit missionaries, is practised by approximately 97 percent of the population, and the liturgical calendar shapes community life: Easter processions wind through Dili's streets, village patron saint festivals fill the highlands with music and shared meals, and Christmas draws families together nationwide. At the table, Portuguese influence appears in pastéis (filled pastries), crusty wheat bread baked in wood-fired ovens, and the strong sweet coffee culture that links Timorese highland arabica to a distinctly Lusophone way of drinking it.
For travellers from the Lusophone world, Timor-Leste is a revelation. For everyone else, the Portuguese dimension adds a layer of cultural complexity and historical depth that makes this small nation unlike anywhere else in Southeast Asia.
